stem: At a routine postpartum visit, the client says mood is ‘fine’ and reports no psychiatric history. Which approach to depression and anxiety screening is appropriate?

options.A: Screen only when the client reports persistent sadness, loss of interest, or another symptom suggesting a postpartum mood disorder.
options.B: Omit postpartum screening if depression screening was already completed during pregnancy.
options.C: Refer all mood screening to a mental-health specialist rather than using validated tools in obstetric care.
options.D: Screen for depression and anxiety with a standardized, validated instrument and have systems for timely assessment and follow-up.

rationale: ACOG recommends that everyone receiving postpartum care be screened for depression and anxiety using standardized, validated instruments. Screening should be implemented with systems that ensure timely assessment and diagnosis, effective treatment, and appropriate monitoring and follow-up according to severity. Therefore D is correct even when the client does not volunteer symptoms or a psychiatric history.
educational_objective: Provide routine postpartum depression and anxiety screening with a standardized, validated instrument and ensure a system exists for timely assessment, treatment, monitoring, and follow-up.
source_organization: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG)
source_document_title: Clinical Practice Guideline No. 4: Screening and Diagnosis of Mental Health Conditions During Pregnancy and Postpartum; Patient Screening
source_version_date: June 2023 CPG; current ACOG screening page accessed 2026-08-16
source_locator: ACOG Patient Screening — recommendations from Clinical Practice Guideline 4: everyone receiving postpartum care screened for depression/anxiety using standardized validated instruments; screening at postpartum visits; systems for timely assessment/diagnosis, treatment, monitoring and follow-up.
source_claim_supported: Routine postpartum depression and anxiety screening is recommended for all patients using standardized validated instruments, with systems for timely assessment, treatment and follow-up.

source_original.stem: At a routine postpartum visit, the client says mood is “fine” and reports no psychiatric history. Which approach to depression and anxiety screening is appropriate?

options.A: Screen when the client reports persistent sadness, loss of interest, or another symptom suggesting a postpartum mood disorder.
options.B: Omit postpartum screening if depression screening was already completed during pregnancy.
options.C: Refer all mood screening to a mental-health specialist rather than using validated tools in obstetric care.
options.D: Screen for depression and anxiety with a validated instrument and have systems for timely assessment and follow-up.

source_original.rationale: ACOG recommends screening patients receiving postpartum care for depression and anxiety with standardized, validated instruments and having systems in place for timely assessment, treatment, and follow-up. Option D matches that guidance even when the client does not volunteer symptoms. Option A incorrectly limits screening to symptomatic clients. Option B omits recommended postpartum screening. Option C incorrectly removes screening from routine obstetric care.
source_original.source_detail: ACOG Clinical Practice Guideline No. 4 / Patient Screening — screen everyone receiving postpartum care for depression and anxiety using standardized validated instruments, with systems for assessment, treatment, monitoring and follow-up. ACOG Clinical Practice Guideline No. 4, June 2023, retained as current guidance; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Health Promotion and Maintenance; preventive care, screening, prenatal/postpartum and newborn health-promotion activities as applicable. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: The clinical construct and key were retained. Option A was tightened from ‘screen when symptomatic’ to ‘screen only when symptomatic’ so it is unambiguously inconsistent with universal postpartum screening. The source locator was tied directly to ACOG CPG 4 recommendations reproduced on the current Patient Screening page.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Routine postpartum depression and anxiety screening
audit_findings.source_authority: Current official ACOG CPG-derived screening guidance.
audit_findings.currentness: ACOG Patient Screening page and CPG 4 rechecked 2026-08-16.
audit_findings.exact_locator: Patient Screening recommendation list reproduces the exact postpartum screening and systems requirements.
audit_findings.claim_audit: No specific named instrument, screening score, treatment threshold, or timing beyond postpartum visits was imposed.

distractor_audit.A: Incorrect because screening is routine for all postpartum-care recipients, not only symptomatic patients.
distractor_audit.B: Incorrect because ACOG recommends postpartum screening even when screening occurred during pregnancy.
distractor_audit.C: Incorrect because validated screening belongs within obstetric care workflows; specialty referral is not a prerequisite to screening.
distractor_audit.D: Correct and matches both universal screening and systems requirements.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only D satisfies both routine screening and follow-up-system requirements.
audit_findings.cueing: All options are screening-policy statements of similar structure.
audit_findings.blueprint: Fits Health Promotion and Maintenance through postpartum preventive screening.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Second-pass review specifically checked that option A could not be interpreted as compatible opportunistic screening in addition to routine screening; ‘only’ removes that ambiguity.
